body.text: They are streets ahead of us in the economy. There is nothing we can do about that, except move from envy and jealousy to celebrating their achievement. In education, they stole a march over us decades ago and have only kept improving. This is also the case with health and nutrition. “Swachch Cheen” is not a slogan but a lived reality. As for income per capita, they are soaring like an eagle and we can only shade our eyes to see them soar higher and higher.

Technologically, there is no cutting edge they have not arrived at long before us. Even if there are sectors in which we might narrow or even eliminate the gap, across the broader technological front they are unassailable. And although our sightseeing venues are arguably more diverse and attractive, or certainly comparable, the numbers flocking to China are far greater.

Roads and communication infrastructure: again, what they have already achieved, we can only aspire to. The skies there are blue, and the air can be breathed. They are also a formidable military power and have shown themselves in Operation Sindoor to be military allies of Pakistan. And much as we might love to devise ways of overwhelming them or even circumventing them, the fact is that we are not in the same league and can get there only at enormous cost to the welfare and development of our people.

Should we remain mired in regret and disappointment, or shall we think of China’s progress as a key opening to our own progress? After all, we are their largest neighbour, at least in South Asia. But rather than looking at opportunities to benefit ourselves from Chinese progress, we remain diffident even about pragmatic partnerships and cooperation. We approach China hesitantly. We are held back by suspicion and scepticism.

Nevertheless, the logic of the marketplace is so compulsive that despite our restrictive trade policy towards China, the market has ensured that our mutual trade, although heavily weighted towards China, has topped $155 billion and is surging. We buy not because we are idle hedonists but because these imports generate employment, growth, and diversification in our economy. It is more important to promote healthy cooperation than remain ever-watchful of perfidy.

I am not a China expert. I am glad I am not. For had I been one, my mind would have been so filled with complex ideograms as to come in the way of clear thinking. For the China-India relationship is so tangled that for every step forward, there is good reason to take two steps back, and for every step backwards, there are at least two good reasons why we should be going forward. Unsurprisingly, the most difficult choice for a Prime Minister is deciding what the goal should be and then not let it get caught in a web of alternative choices.
Rajiv Gandhi and China

I was with Rajiv Gandhi on his famous 1988 visit to China. I was merely a speech-writer. Although I tendered no advice and was content to clothe in words what I took to be the Prime Minister’s thoughts, my drafts were subjected to such intense scrutiny by the China experts that it required several interventions by the Prime Minister to keep the drafts on track. The experts took at least 12 drafts to reluctantly clear what might have taken the Prime Minister one to signal his approval.

Thus, at the end of the day, expert advice is so often so contradictory, even eccentric, that the decision-maker has to be clear as to what he wants. The goal itself—the restoration of peaceful coexistence with China—must be clearly and unambiguously articulated. If not, expert advice will only leave the decision-maker confused as to what his or her larger objective should be.

This was the situation that Rajiv inherited from his mother, Indira Gandhi, who was clear that peaceful coexistence must be restored, but her senior advisers were from the generation that had been so traumatised by 1962 that their policy boiled down to objecting that normalcy with China was tantamount to forgiving China’s “betrayal” of her father. Uninformed public prejudice has always distorted our national priorities with respect to China.

Rajiv Gandhi, who had little to do with his mother’s generation, first put that generation out to grass and then set his team, led by Gopi Arora, to fashion a policy that would be directed at converting the relationship from “managed coexistence” to “peaceful coexistence”, as pointed out by former National Security Adviser M.K. Narayanan.

According to Narayanan, this clarity of goals brought about “a new watershed in relations” after 34 years of grey dusk and became “a beacon of light” that shines “to this day”. Rajiv Gandhi and Deng Xiaoping agreed to discuss the “border question” separately through Special Envoys to sidestep “bureaucratic hurdles” and “military confidence-building measures”. Unfortunately, the present government has “frittered away” the opportunity.

On the eve of going to China, Rajiv signalled from an international platform that his aim was to “establish a relationship between our countries commensurate with the contribution which the two civilisations have made to world history”.

In Beijing, he clarified further that the need of the hour was to make the level of cooperation “commensurate with the contribution which we must together make to the building of a new world order”—a veritable Asian G-2.

To get there, the boundary question must not remain “a major problem” but be “settled amicably, within a realistic time-frame”. Meanwhile, there must be “peace and tranquillity” on the border, and so there was for three long decades. But I don’t think his “realistic time-frame” meant four wasted decades without a settlement. Tragically, no Prime Minister has clearly instructed his Special Envoy to settle or perish. So, peace and tranquillity have withered. The delay has compounded the problem. The experts have prevailed.

Publicly, Rajiv laid out the goals. Privately, he pursued them at the highest level with his Chinese counterpart. I would suggest that the greatest achievement of the visit was Deng shaking hands with Rajiv for what one count recorded as 81/2 minutes! The handshake signalled what the Heads wanted their experts to work out.
Stuck in the past

We are caught in a time warp, forcing history back to where the British left it. Their policy with regard to our Himalayan borders was ever “flexible frontiers”, based on how far they could push forward at a time when neither the effete Tsarists nor China could push back. Now, the People’s Republic of China can.

Instead of relying on inherited myths, let us understand what is vital to us and, therefore, negotiable, rather than insisting that what’s mine is mine and what is yours is also mine. If Aksai Chin was always ours, why have we never had a District Magistrate posted there? Is it not true that “not a blade of grass” grows in the cold, forbidding desert that is the plateau?

For the Chinese, on the other hand, the plateau is the vital link between its two most troubled regions: Sinkiang and Tibet. Moreover, in all its long history, Tibet has exercised its sovereignty only for 40. We, on the other hand, need Arunachal Pradesh, which has never been Chinese. More than 60 years ago, Premier Zhou Enlai was ready to accept our claim to the North-East Frontier Agency or NEFA, as Arunachal Pradesh was then called. It is we who declined. At which the Chinese occupied it in 1962. And vacated it of their own volition within a month, all their conquered lands, including Tawang.

So, let us unambiguously let the Chinese know the limits of our national interests. And then we might follow the other 13 neighbours of China who have settled their border disputes with the country on such pragmatic grounds. The longer we wait, the more intractable the problems grow.

Mani Shankar Aiyar served 26 years in the Indian Foreign Service, is a four-time MP with over two decades in Parliament, and was a Cabinet Minister from 2004 to 2009. He has published nine books; the latest is A Maverick in Politics, the second part of his memoir.
